rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Road to the Mountain
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a tin owl hopping gravely beside a shaggy straw bear along a dusty country road, a small green monkey leaping ahead with a little canary riding on his shoulder, wheat fields and hedgerows, soft afternoon light with long shadows, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: The four friends left Ku-Klip's shop in the morning: a tin owl hopping gravely, a straw bear rustling at every step, a green monkey springing over the stile, and a little canary singing on the monkey's shoulder. Anybody watching would have seen four strange animals. The friends themselves saw exactly who they were. Woot was beginning to like his tail, which curled when he was pleased.

"It feels odd to walk on fur," said Woot, turning a somersault to try it out. "But I shall get used to it, if you will all get used to me." "We got used to a boy who asks questions," said the Scarecrow-bear. "A monkey who asks questions is only a small change." The Scarecrow had to stop himself from patting Woot's head, because friends used to be taller.
Four changed friends walk the long road together.

They walked all day across the Munchkin plain, and at evening they slept in a haystack, and Polychrome sang them a little rainbow song. Her song had all seven colors in it, if songs can have colors, and they decided this one could. In the night the tin owl watched the stars, because owls keep odd hours. Once or twice he said "who" in his round owl voice, just to be proper about it. And the road went on and on under the moon.
Ask your child: every one of them is in the wrong shape, and every one of them is still himself. How do friends know each other anyway?

At last they climbed a low green mountain, and from the top Woot pointed with a furry paw. "Look! Smoke from a chimney. Somebody's home." And below them, small as a toy, lay a cottage with a garden full of flowers. "Then let us go and knock," said the tin owl softly.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Nimmie Amee's Door
chapters.artPrompt: a kind Munchkin woman with a bright apron welcoming a green monkey, a straw bear, a tin owl and a little canary through a cottage garden gate, flowering beans and roses around, bright happy morning light, warm storybook illustration

blocks.text: The cottage garden was full of flowers and bean vines and busy bees. At the gate stood a kind Munchkin woman with a bright apron. When she saw a monkey, a bear, an owl and a canary arriving together, she laughed before she could help it, and her laugh was as bright as her apron. "Well! What a parade." The canary fluttered to her shoulder at once, because birds know who is kind.

"Good morning, ma'am," said Woot, making his best bow. "We are strange-looking travelers with kind errands. We have come a long way to see Nimmie Amee. And some of us have loved her for a very long time indeed." The woman's laugh stopped. "I am Nimmie Amee," she said quietly. Her eyes went soft, and her voice went strange.
Nimmie Amee welcomes her strange visitors to the garden.

She brought out chairs and little cakes. Soon they had told her everything. The woodman and the enchanted axe, the soldier and the enchanted sword. The long road, and the witch who changed their shapes. Woot told most of it, and Polychrome sang a little of it, which made it prettier and only slightly less true. Nimmie Amee listened with her hands folded, the way you listen to something that matters.
Ask your child: Nimmie Amee cannot see her old friends inside the owl and the bear. What tells her they are true friends anyway?

"Two tin men loved me," she said at last, looking from the owl to the bear. "And here they are, in feathers and straw, come all this way to ask after me." "That is the kindest news I have had in years." She stood up and smoothed her apron, and her cheeks went pink. "But there is something you must know."

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Chopfyt Comes Home
chapters.artPrompt: a plain kindly man with a stiff, patched look carrying wooden chairs into a cottage garden, a green monkey, a straw bear and a tin owl watching from a garden table, a Munchkin woman smiling at the cottage door, golden evening light, gently funny storybook illustration

blocks.text: "In a few days," said Nimmie Amee, "I am to be married." "Married!" cried Woot, nearly falling off the gate. "To whom?" "To a quiet man called Chopfyt," she said. "Ku-Klip the tinsmith made him out of spare parts. He grumbles a little, but he is good, and he stays." The monkey's tail curled tight, and even the canary went quiet.

Just then footsteps came up the path, and in walked a stiff-jointed man with a plain, honest face. "Guests!" he grumbled. "Now I must fetch more chairs, and the chairs are heavy, and nobody ever thinks about the chairs." But he fetched them anyway, one by one, without being asked twice. Nimmie Amee patted a chair as it went by, the way you would pat an old friend.
Chopfyt grumbles kindly and fetches the chairs.

The tin owl and the straw bear looked at each other for a long, long moment. Spare parts. They remembered the tinsmith's shelves, and every little thing on them, and they said nothing at all about it. "The tinsmith let nothing go to waste," said the owl at last, very gently. Whatever he had been made from, he was kind to her, and kindness is the part that matters.
New word: spare parts — extra pieces kept in case they are needed. Ku-Klip never threw anything away. What does your family keep in its strangest drawer?

Soon the tea was poured, and Chopfyt explained, at length and with great feeling, exactly how the chairs ought to be arranged. Nimmie Amee smiled at her guests across the table. Her smile said it again, plain as print: this grumbling, faithful man was her choice. And she was content. The owl and the bear drank their tea slowly, and their minds were far away and long ago.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Happy Choice
chapters.artPrompt: a kind Munchkin woman standing at her garden gate beside her plain good-natured bridegroom, a tin owl and a straw bear bowing warmly to them both, a green monkey and a little canary watching from a low branch, golden evening light over the flowers, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: That evening the tin owl hopped close to Nimmie Amee and spoke for the bear and himself. "We came to ask you an old question. You loved us once, and we loved you. Would you have one of us now — an owl, or a bear, or the tin man inside either?" The canary held her breath on his shoulder, and the bear held his straw.

Nimmie Amee shook her head, but she was smiling while she did it. "I loved you both," she said. "And then you both went away — not by your own faults, I know that too. Chopfyt stayed. He is here every evening, and he grumbles at the chairs, and he is mine." The word "stayed" sat in the garden like a small warm stone.
The tin owl and the straw bear give their blessing.

The owl and the bear were quiet for a while, and the garden was quiet too. Then the owl said what both of them were thinking. "Then we wish you joy with all our hearts. Your happiness is the best ending we could have found." Somewhere a bee went on working, because bees do not stop for love stories.
Ask your child: neither tin man got the answer he came for. Why are they smiling anyway? Talk about how wishing someone well can be a gift you give yourself.

"A heart is for making other people happy," the owl added, "and yours is doing fine work." And Nimmie Amee laughed her bright laugh and shook each of their paws in turn. There was a wedding soon after, with cake for everyone. Even the monkey ate his slice and wanted more. And the two tin friends danced a slow, careful dance on the grass, which everyone said was the shiniest thing ever seen in that garden.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Back to the Emerald City
chapters.artPrompt: a graceful girl-queen with a slender wand in a bright emerald hall as sparkles of magic swirl around, a boy in traveling clothes blinking in surprise, a scarecrow straightening his hat and a tall tin man beginning to shine, a rainbow-colored girl laughing beside them, joyful warm light, magical storybook illustration

blocks.text: The four friends walked home slowly, the way they had come. "I am glad we went," said the straw bear, rustling along. "A question answered is a lighter thing to carry than a question wondered about. My straw feels fluffier already." "That is the wind," said the tin owl. "It feels like the same thing." Woot swung through the low branches for practice, in case he missed his tail later.

In the Emerald City, Ozma was waiting on the palace steps. She looked at the owl, the bear, the monkey and the canary for a long moment, and her eyes twinkled. "Dear me," she said. "I think some of my friends have borrowed the wrong shapes. Come in, all of you." Woot bowed as well as a monkey can, which is surprisingly well.
Ozma gives everyone back their own shapes.

She waved her wand, and the wrong shapes rolled away like morning fog. Woot stood in his own shoes, blinking at his own hands. His tail was gone, and he found, a little to his surprise, that he missed it. The Scarecrow fluffed his straw and straightened his hat. The Tin Woodman shone brighter than ever, and gave one joyful squeak of hinges. And Polychrome's colors came out again, like a ribbon unrolling.
Ask your child: which friend was most glad to be himself again? Describe the very moment the magic lifted — what would it feel like, sound like, look like?

That night there was a feast in the palace, and the Tin Woodman told the whole story, all the way to the wedding cake. Woot ate four slices, by way of saying thank you. Everybody agreed it was a very good ending. "The best kind," said Ozma. "Nobody got exactly what they wanted, and everybody got what they needed."

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Woot Says Goodbye
chapters.artPrompt: a tall shining tin man and a small boy with a knapsack shaking hands at a green garden gate, the Emerald City towers behind and an open country road ahead, a scarecrow waving from the wall, bright morning light, warm farewell storybook illustration

blocks.text: After a few happy days, Woot the Wanderer grew restless, the way wanderers do. He stood by the garden gate in the morning sun, looking down the road that went on and on. His knapsack was packed, and a dozen adventures were already queuing up in his head. "The world is large," he said, "and I have only seen a bit of it so far."

The Tin Woodman walked out to the gate with him. "You asked me one small question," he said, "and it carried me a long way. Whatever became of Nimmie Amee? Now I know the answer. And it is a better answer than the one I was hoping for." Ku-Klip's shop, the giantess's castle, a bear's straw, a monkey's tail — he counted them off like old friends.
The Tin Woodman says goodbye to Woot at the gate.

"That was the answer you were really looking for," said Woot. "I thought so all along." The Tin Woodman patted the boy's shoulder very gently, because tin fingers are strong. Woot promised to come back and tell him about the world, a bit at a time. "And I shall want to hear about everything," laughed Woot, "starting with whatever is over the next hill." The garden gate clicked shut behind them, friendly as ever.
Ask your child: the Tin Woodman set out to find a bride and came home with something else instead. What did he find? Talk about answers that turn out better than the ones we hope for.

Off went Woot down the road, whistling, with his knapsack and the whole world in front of him. The Tin Woodman watched until the road curved away. Then he walked back to his shining castle, where his friend the Scarecrow was waiting with questions of his own. He thought about tin hearts, and gardens, and questions that take their time.
